slides.say: a is an integer. Given: a is bigger than one and smaller than two hundred, and a has exactly three different divisors, including one and a. How many different values can a have?
The whole question hides in one given, exactly three divisors. And we've seen this one before. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, with the rule, and then with trial and error to find the pattern.
[short pause] Remember, divisors come in pairs, and exactly three divisors means a prime squared. One, the prime, and the prime squared, like nine, with one, three and nine.

We're choosing the prime whose square will be a. The upper limit of two hundred applies to that square. So a is a prime squared, and a is less than two hundred. How big can the prime be? Fourteen squared is a hundred ninety-six, still below two hundred. Fifteen squared is two hundred twenty-five, too big. So the prime is fourteen or less.

Each allowed prime produces one different value of a, so counting the primes will count the possible values of a. The primes up to fourteen are two, three, five, seven, eleven and thirteen. Six of them. Their squares are four, nine, twenty-five, forty-nine, a hundred twenty-one and a hundred sixty-nine, all below two hundred.
So a has six values, and choice number three is our answer.
at: choice number three is our answer

slides.say: Now careful, a lot of students stop at the one-digit primes, two, three, five and seven, and answer four, choice number four. But eleven squared and thirteen squared are still below two hundred.

[pause] Another way is trial and error. Don't remember the rule? Run through the numbers, count the divisors, and look for the pattern. Two and three are prime, two divisors each. Four has one, two and four. Three divisors, the first one that fits. Five is prime. Six has one, two, three and six, that's four. Seven is prime. Eight has one, two, four and eight, four again.
at: Four has one, two and four

slides.say: Nine has one, three and nine. It fits.

Stop and look for the pattern. Four is two squared, and nine is three squared, squares of primes. But careful, not every square. Sixteen is four squared, and it has one, two, four, eight and sixteen, five divisors, because four isn't a prime.

So the next ones are five squared, twenty-five, seven squared, forty-nine, eleven squared, a hundred twenty-one, and thirteen squared, a hundred sixty-nine. Seventeen squared is two hundred eighty-nine, too big. Six values, choice number three. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
